architecture_decisions.decision: Python stdlib http.server + sqlite3 for backend, single static HTML+vanilla JS file for frontend. No external dependencies (sandbox has no network access).
No schema edit was needed because the existing implementation meets db-1; an isolated SQLite initialization check passed.
No server edit was needed; existing handlers validate input, persist changes through SQLite, and return JSON task records.
`python3 -m unittest -v test_api.py` passed all 8 tests, including protected create/list/update/delete lifecycle coverage.
No frontend edit was needed; `static/index.html` meets fe-1 while preserving the existing authenticated API flow and vanilla-JS-only constraint.
Validated with `python3 -m unittest -v test_api.py`: 8/8 passing.
Validated `database.py` and `server.py` syntax with `py_compile`; inspected static UI endpoint wiring and all three board columns.
Recorded the full-suite errors as test-environment/orchestrator failures because they are outside the Sprint 1 app paths and their traces do not implicate the Kanban implementation.
No security patch is required for the scoped local app.
Verified all 8 API/security regression tests pass, including token tampering/expiry rejection, cross-user mutation denial, password hashing, login-work equalization, and CSP without unsafe-inline.
The server intentionally binds to localhost and requires a 32-byte KANBAN_JWT_SECRET before startup.
Retain the standard-library stack: http.server, sqlite3, json, hashlib, hmac, and vanilla JavaScript in one static HTML file.
Use PBKDF2-HMAC with random per-user salts for passwords and signed, expiring HS256 JWTs; require an application signing secret at startup.
Enforce task ownership on the server for list, create, update, and delete operations; unauthenticated requests receive 401 and cross-user task access is treated as not found.
The existing graph is acyclic: arch-2 → db-2 → be-2 → fe-2 → qa-2/security-2. No additional task is needed.
Use Python standard-library components only: sqlite3, hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac, hmac-SHA256, http.server, and vanilla JavaScript.
Passwords use PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with a random salt per user; the server must require a sufficiently strong JWT signing secret at startup.
JWTs contain integer subject, issued-at, and expiry claims; accept HS256 only and compare signatures in constant time.
Return 401 for missing/invalid authentication and 404 for another user's task, preventing task-existence disclosure.
The planned dependency chain is valid and introduces no file ownership overlap: database.py → server.py → static/index.html.
No database edit was needed: the existing migration adds nullable tasks.user_id for legacy databases and preserves existing task rows.
An isolated legacy-database migration check confirmed users creation, user_id addition, ownership index creation, and legacy task preservation.
No server edit was needed: existing standard-library code uses PBKDF2-HMAC password derivation, HS256 signing with expiry validation, and user-scoped task SQL.
Four focused authentication and authorization regression tests passed.
No frontend edit was needed; the existing single static HTML file meets the authentication contract without external dependencies.
The interface keeps user-visible account data in page memory and persists only the JWT for the current browser session.
No new test file was needed because the existing focused suite covers the Sprint 2 acceptance paths.
`database.py` and `server.py` also pass Python syntax compilation.
No security patch is required for the scoped localhost app.
Four focused security tests passed: tampered/expired token rejection, cross-user task denial, unknown-user login work equalization, and CSP without unsafe-inline.
Parameterized SQLite queries, bounded JSON input, strict field validation, and textContent-based rendering reduce injection risks.
Keep the existing Python standard-library and single-file vanilla-JS architecture.
Search is case-insensitive title matching scoped to the authenticated user; filtering applies a valid status; sorting uses a server-side fixed allowlist rather than client-provided SQL.
Use explicit deterministic defaults: no filter, empty query, and newest-created-first ordering.
The manager graph is acyclic: arch-3 → be-3 → fe-3 → qa-3/security-3. Existing schema fields cover this feature, so no database task is needed.
Use a case-insensitive, bounded title substring search scoped to the authenticated user.
Accept only status values todo, in_progress, done and a fixed server-side sort allowlist; reject malformed or unsupported query parameters with 400.
Default behavior remains unfiltered results ordered newest first; no database schema change is required.
The existing graph is acyclic and preserves ownership boundaries: server.py for backend and static/index.html for frontend.
Search is case-insensitive, limited to 100 characters, and treats %, _, and backslashes literally.
All query values use bound parameters; sort clauses come exclusively from a fixed server-side allowlist.
Listing remains scoped to the authenticated user_id before search and filter conditions.
The UI sends only non-default supported query values, leaving the backend as the validation authority.
Search input is capped at 100 characters to match the API contract; responsive layout collapses the controls on small screens.
Targeted frontend auth/CSP checks and static search-control wiring checks passed.
Added `test_task_search_filter_sort_and_user_isolation` to protect the Sprint 3 API contract.
Validated with `python3 -m unittest -v test_api.py`: 9/9 tests passed.
No security patch is required.
Verified the new search/filter/sort isolation test passes.
Frontend uses URLSearchParams for query encoding and textContent for rendered API content, preserving the existing XSS protections.
Use native HTML drag-and-drop in the existing single static HTML file; do not introduce dependencies.
Only a task ID and a target status are client-side drag state; derive targets from fixed board columns and treat server responses as authoritative.
Optimistic updates change local task state first, then PATCH the authenticated endpoint; on failure restore the previous status and rerender.
The graph is acyclic: arch-4 → be-4 → fe-4 → qa-4/security-4. No schema change is needed.
Drag data contains only the task ID; the destination status comes from a fixed column attribute, not arbitrary drop payload.
Ignore drops onto the task's current column.
The server remains authoritative: an optimistic success may be reconciled from the PATCH response, while a failed request must restore the exact prior local task list/state.
No task graph changes are required; the existing dependencies are acyclic and file ownership remains separated.
No backend edit was needed: PATCH validates statuses, scopes updates by authenticated user_id, and returns non-2xx errors suitable for frontend rollback.
Focused protected-lifecycle and user-isolation regression tests passed.
Drops onto a task's existing status are ignored.
A failed PATCH restores a copied pre-move task state; a 401 keeps the existing signed-out behavior.
Verified static drag/drop and optimistic-update wiring, plus existing frontend authentication and CSP checks.

Added a static interaction-contract test because the standard-library-only project has no browser automation harness; it verifies draggable cards, fixed drop targets, optimistic render before PATCH, and rollback after PATCH failure.
Added an API regression ensuring an invalid status update returns 400 without changing the stored task.
Validated with `python3 -m unittest -v test_api.py`: 11/11 tests passed.
No security patch is required.
Verified focused drag/drop contract, invalid-status rejection, and protected lifecycle tests pass.
External drag payload is ignored because drops act only when an in-memory dragTaskId was set by an application card.
The planner begins with a finite, frozen task graph; only architect-validated recovery tasks may be appended after the repeated-blocker threshold.
A recovery task must target the blocking work, carry a valid owner and existing dependency relation, and never introduce a dependency cycle.
When a dependency is blocked, pause downstream tasks; when recovery completes, resume only tasks whose dependencies are satisfied.
Persist task transitions, reassignments, recovery links, and replanning events atomically so dashboard replay derives from durable state.
No database task is required. The graph is acyclic: arch-5 → be-5 → fe-5 → qa-5/security-5.
Keep initial planning finite and frozen; autonomous task generation is reserved for architect-valid recovery work.
Pause downstream dependencies when work is blocked, then resume only after recovery and dependency completion.
Persist all adaptive events atomically so reloads and dashboard replay have deterministic state.
The existing task graph is acyclic and sufficient; no database task or dependency change is required.

No orchestrator edit was needed because `orchestrator/run.py` already enforces repeated-blocker thresholds, avoids duplicate recovery tasks, validates recovery dependencies against cycles, pauses/resumes dependent work, and persists adaptive events.
Ran six focused adaptive orchestration and dashboard replay tests successfully.
No dashboard edit was needed: persisted replanning events feed activity and replay, task chips render paused/blocked/reassigned state, and blockers display recovery status.
Five focused dashboard replay and safe-rendering tests passed.
No new test file was needed because the existing focused adaptive, dashboard replay, and commit-safety suites cover the Sprint 5 acceptance paths.
`orchestrator/run.py` passes Python syntax compilation.
Recovered a concrete validation gap: previously add_tasks only rejected duplicate IDs, allowing malformed owners or dangling dependencies from dynamic proposals.
Recovery tasks remain architect-owned and cycle-validated; the new gate also prevents invalid proposal data from entering durable state.
